articles.title: Wall Street posts its best day since April 2025 as Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang, recouping over half of last week's rout
articles.excerpt: The S&P 500 jumped 4.7% and the Nasdaq 6.5% after Nvidia's board brought its founder back as CEO, ending a seven-day S&P losing streak and adding about $950 billion to the chipmaker's market value in one session.
articles.author: fiveboroughbulletin-staff
articles.imageCaption: The New York Stock Exchange on Wall Street, where U.S. stocks staged their best day since April 2025 on Monday
articles.imageAlt: The columned facade of the New York Stock Exchange with a large American flag, where U.S. stocks surged on Monday after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang
content: Wall Street staged its strongest rally in more than a year on Monday after Nvidia's board reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as chief executive, reversing a punishing sell-off that had pushed the S&P 500 and the Dow into correction territory. The S&P 500 jumped 4.7 percent, the Nasdaq Composite rose 6.5 percent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained nearly 1,450 points, or 3 percent, according to the [Associated Press](https://www.irishnews.com/news/world/us-stocks-surge-after-jensen-huang-returns-as-nvidias-chief-executive-TZ4G7S63IJIW7FSLCTPQCNVNMU/). The S&P 500 finished at roughly 7,237, ending a seven-day losing streak, and both it and the Nasdaq posted their best day since April 2025, when President Donald Trump paused most of his Liberation Day tariffs. [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/23/business/live-news/jensen-huang-reinstated-as-ceo-of-nvidia) noted that the Dow's advance was its strongest since Nov. 4, when stocks rallied after the midterm elections.

Nvidia was both the catalyst and the biggest winner. Its shares surged 31.5 percent to close at $165.05, according to [Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/u-stock-futures-steady-nvidia-004836470.html), adding about $950 billion in market value in a single session, which [NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/business/markets/stocks-rebound-ai-tech-selloff-nvidia-rcna610833) described as the largest one-day gain in market capitalization any company has recorded. [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/23/anthropic-nvidia-shares.html) said it was the stock's best day since May 2003 and followed a slump of more than 40 percent over the previous month. Even so, Nvidia remains about 30 percent below its early-October record, NBC reported. The buying was broad, with 26 of the 30 Dow components finishing higher, and shares of CoreWeave, which rents out cloud access to Nvidia chips, shot up 22.3 percent, the AP said.

The reversal capped a dramatic two weeks for the chipmaker. Huang resigned on Nov. 12 after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a Megaspeed executive suspected of being a Chinese agent, [Yahoo Finance reported](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/live/stock-market-today-monday-november-23-dow-sp-500-nasdaq-nvidia-reinstates-jensen-huang-141511975.html). Less than a week before Monday's announcement the board had turned down an offer from Huang to return, the AP said; this time it voted unanimously to restore him as CEO, president and board director, effective immediately. The board said it had received input from senior levels of the U.S. government and is confident his return poses no national security risk, although its independent investigation into his ties to the Megaspeed executive will continue and a new National Security and Export Control Committee has been formed. The board had opened an [independent inquiry led by a former federal prosecutor](/business/nvidia-hires-ex-prosecutor-lead-huang-probe-shares-slide) only days before Huang stepped down.

Washington's role is a large part of the story. President Trump had publicly urged the board to bring Huang back, and he told CNBC on Monday, "I believe my intervention was very important," the [AP](https://www.irishnews.com/news/world/us-stocks-surge-after-jensen-huang-returns-as-nvidias-chief-executive-TZ4G7S63IJIW7FSLCTPQCNVNMU/) reported. [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/23/business/live-news/jensen-huang-reinstated-as-ceo-of-nvidia) framed the reinstatement as coming under pressure from the president, a point that may keep questions about the board's independence alive even as the stock recovers.

Monday's gains erased only part of last week's damage. The Nasdaq fell 10 percent last week, its worst week since the early days of Covid in 2020, [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/23/anthropic-nvidia-shares.html) reported, leaving all three major averages in correction territory and the Nasdaq negative for 2026. The S&P 500 dropped 3.7 percent on Friday alone, to 6,910.39, according to [Schwab](https://www.schwab.com/learn/story/stock-market-update-open), and Yahoo Finance estimated that about $8 trillion had been wiped from the index since its Oct. 6 peak. The AP calculated that U.S. stocks recovered just over half of last week's loss, and the Nasdaq-100 is still almost 15 percent below its last record, NBC News noted. One AI name sat out the rally: Anthropic, which [priced its IPO at $83 a share](/finance/anthropic-prices-ipo-at-83-a-share-above-range-1-5-trillion-valuation-nasdaq-debut), was down about 1.7 percent and below $88 late Monday morning after a 17 percent debut-day jump and a 9 percent drop on Friday, Yahoo Finance said.

Strategists cautioned against reading the move as an all-clear. Nomura's Charlie McElligott said much of the surge reflected forced buying as short sellers covered and options dealers unwound hedges, and he warned that stubborn inflation, rising borrowing costs and cooling expectations for corporate AI spending have not gone away, [Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/live/stock-market-today-monday-november-23-dow-sp-500-nasdaq-nvidia-reinstates-jensen-huang-141511975.html) reported. The AP said Monday's strength could easily give way to more losses, pointing to fears of an AI bubble, the prospect of tougher regulation from a Democratic-controlled Congress and high bond yields that make the AI build-out costlier to finance. On the other side of the ledger, S&P 500 companies are on track for third-quarter earnings growth of nearly 33 percent, according to FactSet figures cited by the AP, and Barclays analysts wrote that the risks should make the AI build-out slower and more selective rather than derail it.

Attention now turns to the Federal Reserve and a holiday-shortened week. Traders see about a 96 percent chance of a quarter-point rate increase at the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool as cited by [Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/u-stock-futures-steady-nvidia-004836470.html). On Wednesday, the October core PCE inflation reading is forecast at 3.2 percent from a year earlier, up from 3.1 percent, alongside third-quarter GDP and the Fed's Beige Book, [FXStreet](https://www.fxstreet.com/news/us-stock-indices-rebound-as-nvidia-reinstates-jensen-huang-202611232157) said. U.S. markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving and shut at 1 p.m. Eastern on Friday, [Proactive Investors](https://www.proactiveinvestors.com/companies/news/1102277/week-ahead-wall-street-looks-for-thanksgiving-lift-as-nvidia-rebound-puts-ai-trade-back-in-focus-1102277.html) noted, and [ABC News](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-24/asx-markets-business-news-live-updates-nov-24-2026/107419524) reported that S&P 500 futures were flat early Tuesday, leaving open whether Monday's surge marks a lasting turn or a short-lived squeeze.

articles.title: Anthropic prices IPO at $83 a share, above its range, valuing Claude maker at $1.5 trillion before Nasdaq debut
articles.excerpt: The AI developer sold 980 million shares above its $70 to $78 range in an offering CNBC puts at $81.3 billion, with trading as ANT set to begin Thursday after Wall Street's fifth straight S&P 500 loss.
articles.author: fiveboroughbulletin-staff
articles.imageCaption: The Nasdaq MarketSite tower in Times Square, where Anthropic shares begin trading Thursday under the ticker ANT
articles.imageAlt: The illuminated Nasdaq MarketSite tower in Times Square at dusk, where Anthropic's IPO shares are set to begin trading
content: Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 a share on Wednesday evening, above the $70 to $78 range it had marketed earlier this month, clearing the way for the Claude maker to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT. In its own [announcement](https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropic-prices-initial-public-offering), the company said the deal covers 980 million Class A shares, of which 956,351,354 are being sold by Anthropic and 23,648,646 by existing stockholders, and that underwriters hold a 30-day option on up to 147 million more. [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/18/anthropic-ipo-ai-offering-price.html) reported that the sale raised $81.3 billion and values the company at roughly $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis.

The offering was increased from the 825 million shares Anthropic first planned to sell. CNBC called it the largest offering on record, ahead of SpaceX's June listing, though the comparison depends on how the totals are counted: [TipRanks](https://www.tipranks.com/news/anthropic-prices-ipo-at-83-setting-up-94-billion-stock-sale) noted that SpaceX's haul reached about $86.2 billion once its underwriters' extra-share option was included. If Anthropic's underwriters take up their full option, the additional 147 million shares would bring in roughly another $12 billion at the IPO price. Separately, [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/anthropic-ipo-ai-boom-nasdaq-debut/) reported that Anthropic is raising another $26 billion at the same price from companies with a stake in the AI race, including AMD, Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.

The pricing marks a steep step up from the $965 billion valuation Anthropic carried after its May funding round, according to [Calcalist](https://www.calcalistech.com/ctechnews/article/ddyq1vva9), and puts it ahead of the $1.25 trillion figure recently attributed to rival OpenAI, which is based on private-market reporting rather than a public listing. CBS News noted that the valuation still falls short of the $2 trillion some IPO watchers had projected earlier this year. At $83, the shares priced about 6.4 percent above the top of the original range, TipRanks reported, and CNBC said demand ran several times the number of shares on offer.

The numbers behind the valuation are large but lopsided. A recent regulatory filing shows Anthropic took in nearly $17 billion in revenue in the third quarter, up 45 percent from the second, CBS News reported, yet the company is not profitable under standard accounting rules. The [Associated Press](https://www.wral.com/news/ap/70b66-anthropic-prices-its-ipo-at-83-per-share-valuing-the-artificial-intelligence-giant-at-1-5-trillion/) said Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which its filings describe as substantial, and has signed leases and other agreements requiring about $900 billion in spending on computing power and infrastructure in the coming years, including $70 billion over the next 12 months. With borrowing getting more expensive, AP noted, an IPO lets the company raise money without adding to that debt.

The listing arrives at an awkward moment for markets. On Wednesday the S&P 500 fell 0.2 percent for a fifth straight session, its longest losing streak since June, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost more than 560 points, or 1.1 percent, and the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.4 percent, according to [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/18/stock-market-today-live-updates.html). [Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/live/stock-market-today-wednesday-november-18-dow-sp-500-nasdaq-nvidia-earnings-anthropic-ipo-143530588.html) reported that UnitedHealth dragged on the Dow after federal regulators proposed an anti-fraud rule affecting insurers, and that Nvidia gave back early gains and fell more than 3 percent at its lows even after reporting third-quarter results that beat Wall Street's expectations. CBS News added that Nvidia shares are down more than 35 percent from their October peak following the sudden exit of chief executive Jensen Huang, and that AI stocks as a group have sold off since July.

Even so, the AP said the higher-than-expected price signals broad investor enthusiasm for AI shares despite the turbulence. Individual investors were expected to receive as much as 20 percent of the offering, and [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/18/anthropic-ipo-retail-investors.html) cited Vanda Research as estimating about $250 million of net retail buying on the first day, roughly double the level seen at the SpaceX debut. Matthew Kennedy, a strategist at Renaissance Capital, told CBS News that a first-day climb to around $100 would amount to a solid pop, while a move toward $140 would suggest AI enthusiasm had come roaring back. AP also noted that the IPO lets employees begin selling vested stock.

Questions about the business model and oversight will follow the shares onto the exchange. Anthropic is a public-benefit corporation, and AP reported that a long-term benefit trust it has set up can elect or remove a majority of the board, a structure that gives ordinary shareholders less control than usual and could steer the company toward choices that do not maximize returns. Newly elected Democrats in Congress have also vowed to crack down on the industry amid a backlash against data centers, AP said, and University of Florida professor Jay Ritter told CBS News that the market is pricing in very lofty expectations that could be hard for management to meet. The first trades on Thursday will show how much of that optimism survives contact with the open market.

articles.title: Dow jumps 1,100 points and S&P 500 posts best day since April as oil slides ahead of inflation report
articles.excerpt: A plunge in crude and a chip-stock rebound recovered much of last week's AI-driven rout, but Tuesday's October CPI now tests whether a December Fed rate hike stays on the table.
articles.author: fiveboroughbulletin-staff
articles.imageCaption: a close-up of an NYSE screen, ticker showing the S&P 500 or Dow in green
articles.imageAlt: a close-up of an NYSE screen, ticker showing the S&P 500 or Dow in green
content: Wall Street staged its sharpest rally in seven months on Monday as a steep drop in oil prices and a bounce in chip stocks erased much of the damage from last week's artificial intelligence sell-off, setting up a high-stakes inflation report on Tuesday morning. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 1,104.02 points, or 2.15 percent, to close at 52,389.75, [Reuters](https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2026/nov/08/stocks-jump-as-oil-tumbles-nvidia-falls-amid-inter/) reported. The S&P 500 rose 2.35 percent to 7,549.94, its best day since April 8, and the Nasdaq Composite climbed 2.74 percent to 25,253.14.

Crude was the main catalyst. Brent futures fell 5.85 percent to settle at $92.57 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate dropped to $86.85, after President Donald Trump told CNN he thought it highly unlikely he would order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the war progress. The [Associated Press](https://www.bnnbloomberg.ca/markets/dow-jones/2026/11/09/world-markets-bounce-back-after-a-recovery-for-ai-stocks-on-wall-street/) noted that Brent has now come down from more than $112 at the start of the month, easing worries that energy costs would keep feeding inflation. The relief was not guaranteed to last: both Washington and Tehran [reported](https://marketscreener.com/news/oil-falls-on-open-as-trump-says-fresh-iran-attacks-unlikely-ce785fd2d081fe21) shipping hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday that some Iranian demands had been unreasonable.

The rebound followed one of the worst stretches for stocks in more than a year. On Thursday, the Dow fell 1,833 points, or 3.4 percent, the S&P 500 dropped about 4.3 percent, and the Nasdaq sank 5.5 percent into correction territory, its worst day since April 2025, [ABC News](https://abcnews.com/Business/dow-plunges-1200-points-shedding-midterm-results-stock/story?id=137880888) reported. That slide came a day after a post-midterm rally, as investors weighed whether Democratic control of Congress could slow the build-out of AI data centers. Nvidia lost about 9 percent that day, and [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/stock-market-selloff-ai-fears.html) reported that the so-called Magnificent 7 collectively lost $1 trillion in market value.

Chip stocks led Monday's recovery. Reuters said an index of semiconductor shares surged 6.9 percent after plunging more than 12 percent the week before, and the S&P 500 rebounded from its biggest weekly drop since April 2025. Nvidia was the notable exception, falling about 4 percent to its lowest close since April 7 as investors questioned CEO Jensen Huang's future following an internal investigation tied to a possible foreign intelligence effort aimed at him. [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/stock-market-today-live-updates.html) said the Dow is now back above where it closed on Election Day, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq remain slightly below.

The calm is likely to be tested quickly. The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases the October Consumer Price Index at 8:30 a.m. ET Tuesday, and economists surveyed by Bloomberg expect a 0.3 percent monthly increase in headline prices and 0.2 percent in the core measure, [NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/business/economy/october-cpi-inflation-report-gas-prices-rcna608386) reported. That would be a clear slowdown from September's 0.6 percent jump, which pushed annual inflation to 3.7 percent. No annual figure will be published for October because last year's government shutdown prevented the collection of price data, a gap that puts extra weight on the month-to-month change.

The data matters because it is the last inflation reading before the Federal Reserve meets on December 8-9. The central bank raised its benchmark rate by a quarter point in September and held it at 3.75 percent to 4 percent in October, according to [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/treasury-yields-inch-lower-as-investors-look-ahead-to-key-jobs-data-.html), and a [much stronger-than-expected October jobs report](https://www.schwab.com/learn/story/stock-market-update-open) on Friday, with employers adding 165,000 positions, lifted expectations of another increase. Market odds of a December hike stood at about 85 percent on Monday afternoon, NBC News reported, and the 10-year Treasury yield has hovered near 4.9 percent.

Strategists say a soft CPI reading may not be enough to change that path. Economists cited by [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/october-cpi-report-2026-inflation.html) said that, short of an unmistakably weak print, the numbers are unlikely to dissuade the Fed from hiking in December, and Fed officials have warned that price pressures first driven by tariffs and the Iran war are spreading to other parts of the economy. A hotter-than-expected report would likely add to rate-hike bets and could pressure the stocks that rallied Monday, particularly the rate-sensitive technology shares that have swung hardest in recent days.

articles.title: Fed Chair Warsh warns inflation progress has stalled in first Jackson Hole address
articles.excerpt: In his highest-profile speech since taking over the central bank, Warsh declined to signal the Fed's next move, and traders raised their bets on a September rate hike.
articles.author: fiveboroughbulletin-staff
content: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh used his first Jackson Hole address as chair to warn that recent progress on inflation may be less durable than it appears, in a speech that offered investors little of the forward guidance many had been hoping for.

Speaking at the Kansas City Fed's annual symposium in Wyoming, roughly a hundred days into his tenure, Warsh acknowledged that summer inflation readings had come in somewhat better than expected but argued the underlying trend has not clearly improved enough to declare victory. He suggested the central bank could still need to raise rates further if price pressures fail to ease in the months ahead.

Warsh was notably light on specifics about the Fed's next steps, telling the audience they could describe his approach as a general outline or a rough map of his thinking, but stopped short of calling it formal forward guidance, a term that carries specific weight in how markets interpret central bank communication.

That ambiguity had an immediate effect on trading floors. Futures markets tracked by the CME Group's FedWatch tool showed the probability of a quarter-point rate increase at the Fed's mid-September meeting roughly double from about a third to near a coin flip in the hours after the speech, as traders repriced the odds of a more hawkish path.

The tone marked a contrast with the Jackson Hole speech delivered by Warsh's predecessor a year earlier, which had leaned dovish and helped fuel a stock market rally. Warsh's more cautious framing instead left investors parsing his remarks for clues rather than taking comfort from a clear signal in either direction.

Economists said the speech reflected the difficult position facing the Fed as it weighs still-elevated inflation against signs of a cooling labor market, a balancing act that has left policymakers publicly divided over whether the next move should be a cut, a hike, or no change at all when the committee meets next month.

articles.title: S&P 500 tops 7,800 for the first time as August rally extends
articles.excerpt: Cooling inflation data and strong corporate earnings pushed all three major U.S. indexes to fresh records within the same trading week.
articles.author: fiveboroughbulletin-staff
content: The S&P 500 closed above 7,800 for the first time this week, extending an August rally that has carried all three major U.S. stock indexes to fresh record territory within the span of a few trading sessions.

The milestone followed the Dow Jones Industrial Average's own first close above 54,000 earlier in the month, while the Nasdaq Composite has repeatedly set new highs of its own as technology shares continued to lead the broader market higher.

Investors pointed to a combination of factors behind the run, chief among them a string of inflation readings that came in cooler than economists had expected, easing some of the pressure that had weighed on markets earlier in the year. Corporate earnings for the second quarter also came in broadly stronger than forecast, particularly among large technology companies whose results carry outsized weight in the major indexes.

Falling oil prices and a partial easing of tensions in the Middle East also helped support risk appetite, traders said, reducing some of the geopolitical premium that had been built into energy and defense-adjacent stocks earlier in the summer.

Even so, strategists cautioned that markets remain sensitive to any signs of a policy shift from the Federal Reserve, noting that a large share of the year's gains have been concentrated in a small number of dominant technology companies. Any disappointment in upcoming earnings from that group, they said, could quickly test the resilience of the broader rally.

Trading volumes were described as moderate for the milestone, consistent with a summer market that has drifted steadily higher rather than surging on any single catalyst, a pattern several analysts said reflects broad but cautious optimism rather than outright exuberance.

articles.title: Treasury doubles bond buybacks as national debt tops $40 trillion for the first time
articles.excerpt: The surprise move came days after the 30-year yield hit its highest level since 2007, and briefly sent longer-term borrowing costs lower.
articles.author: fiveboroughbulletin-staff
content: The U.S. Treasury Department said this week it will at least double the size of its bond buyback operations, a surprise intervention aimed at easing pressure on longer-term borrowing costs after the 30-year yield touched its highest level since 2007.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's department said it would raise the size of each buyback operation to at least $4 billion from $2 billion, targeting securities in the 10-to-30-year range starting in September and running into early November. The announcement came the same week official figures showed the national debt had climbed above $40 trillion for the first time.

The initial market reaction was sharp: the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield fell from around 4.68 percent to as low as 4.63 percent, while the 30-year yield dropped from roughly 5.26 percent to about 5.18 percent, as the prospect of the government stepping in as a larger buyer of its own long-dated debt eased some of the recent selling pressure.

That relief proved only partial. Yields on both securities drifted back up the following day as traders weighed the buyback plan against the broader forces that had pushed borrowing costs higher in the first place, including concerns about a widening budget deficit, inflation that has stayed above the Fed's target, and a wave of corporate bond issuance competing with Treasuries for investor demand.

Analysts described the buyback increase as a targeted, short-term tool rather than a structural fix for the pressures facing the bond market, noting that the government still needs to finance the same underlying deficit regardless of how it manages the mix of debt maturities it issues.

The episode added to a summer of unusually active involvement by the Treasury in the mechanics of the bond market, with officials signaling they are prepared to use further buybacks or other tools if long-term yields continue climbing toward levels that could ripple into mortgage rates and other consumer borrowing costs.

articles.title: Gold climbs to a three-month high as investors brace for Jackson Hole
articles.excerpt: Bullion's steady August climb reflects a mix of central bank buying, bond market jitters and anticipation of the Fed chair's speech.
articles.author: fiveboroughbulletin-staff
articles.imageCaption: Gold bars at a bullion dealer
content: Gold prices climbed to their highest level in more than three months this week, extending a steady run higher through August as investors positioned themselves ahead of the Federal Reserve's Jackson Hole symposium and a fresh round of inflation data.

December gold futures opened Tuesday just above $4,710 an ounce, building on a rally that has taken the metal from around $4,000 at the start of the month to its strongest levels since the spring. The advance has come in fits and starts, with notable jumps following the Treasury's decision to expand its bond buyback program and after minutes from the Fed's most recent policy meeting were released.

Traders pointed to several forces reinforcing the move. Persistent geopolitical tension in the Middle East has kept a steady bid under gold as a traditional haven asset, while uncertainty over the path of interest rates has made the non-yielding metal relatively more attractive compared with bonds whose returns have been swinging along with Treasury market volatility.

Central bank buying has also provided a structural tailwind. Data from the World Gold Council showed official-sector purchases in the second quarter running well above year-earlier levels, as a number of central banks continued to diversify reserves away from a heavy concentration in the U.S. dollar.

Analysts said the timing of the latest high was no coincidence, coming just days before the Fed chair's highly anticipated Jackson Hole remarks and the release of the central bank's preferred inflation gauge. Any signal that the Fed is prepared to hold rates higher for longer, they said, could either dent gold's momentum by lifting the dollar or extend the rally further if it stokes broader market uncertainty.

Precious metals traders cautioned that gold's gains this year have already outpaced expectations set at the start of 2026, and some warned that a sharp reversal is possible if incoming data reduces the current level of economic uncertainty.
